content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the effect of hard examples on the generalisation of robust models. Compared with standard training, the authors find that hard examples have more negative effort in the case of adversarial training. This work also points out that fitting hard adversarial examples has a similar effect to fitting instances with corrupted labels. Compared with directly pruning the hard examples, difficulty proportional label smoothing (DPLS) is proposed to adaptively utilise hard examples without the sacrificing natural accuracy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

This work studies the effect of hard example from different perspectives, including memorisation, generalisation and extracted features.

Weakness:

1. The originality is the main weakness of this paper, because many empirical observations are the same as the ones in "C. Liu et. al. On the impact of hard adversarial instances on overfitting in adversarial training". Many observations in Section 3.2 are not new, including training with removing hard / easy instances and the observation that directly removing hard examples lead to sub-optimality. 

2. The theoretical results are too weak to support the empirical observations and claims in this paper. The linear model studies here is too simple to give some insights about the deep nonlinear neural networks. In addition, the authors do not give justifications about the two assumptions in Corollary 1: $w^T x_1 \geq 0$ and $0 < \epsilon < (d_1 + d_2) / 2$. In addition, it would better if the authors discuss how the difference between $\mathcal{D}_{std}$ and $\mathcal{D}_{adv}$ evolves when $\epsilon$ increases, because the authors claim the hard examples have more negative effect in adversarial training.

3. The proposed algorithm DPLS is an incremental upgrade of label smoothing and is similar to self-adaptive training. Although the authors compare this method with baselines in Table 4, but I doubt the better performance of DPLS on $A^3$ is a result of robust accuracy - clean accuracy trade-off. The baselines may trade clean accuracy to improve robust accuracy by tuning hyper-parameters. In addition, the improvement is marginal (e.g. 53.49% for KD+SWA v.s. 53.71% for DPLS), the authors should run these experiments multiple time and report the performance variance.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity and Quality: this paper is easy to read in general, but some parts can be clearer. For example, "Theorem 1" is the pure calculation, it might be inappropriate to call it a "theorem". The legend of Figure 5 and Figure 6 can be bigger.

Novelty: this is the main concerns. Many parts, especially the empirical observation, are too similar to a existing work, pointed out in the "weakness" part.

Reproducibility: I did not find the code available for this paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: Based on the concerns above, especially the three points in the "weakness" part, I think the contribution of this paper is very incremental and is below the bar for publishing.

content.title: Response to Reviewer nQWa
content.comment:
Thank you for reviewing our manuscript and pointing out novelties and ambiguity in the theory part. We would like to address your concerns and questions.

**Q**: The originality is the main weakness of this paper, because many empirical observations are the same as the ones in "C. Liu et. al. D". Many observations in Section 3.2 are not new, including training with removing hard / easy instances and the observation that directly removing hard examples lead to sub-optimality. \
**A**: In [1], they showed that directly removing hard examples leads to mitigating overfitting but lower robust performance. However, in our empirical analysis, directly removing hard examples leads to an increase in robustness, which is a different result from [1]. Furthermore, our proposed method directly uses the difficulty of each example to mitigate the negative effect of hard examples on training and improves the test robustness performance. For the comparison study and other experiments, please refer to the response to Reviewer HeMq.

**Q**: The theoretical results are too weak to support the empirical observations and claims in this paper. The linear model studies here is too simple to give some insights about the deep nonlinear neural networks. In addition, the authors do not give justifications about the two assumptions in Corollary 1. In addition, it would be better if the authors discuss how the difference between differences evolves when $\epsilon$ increases. \
**A**:  $w^Tx_1 \geq 0$ represents that the model fits clean example $x$ and correctly classify them. For the condition of the $\epsilon$, considering that $\epsilon$ is the minimum upper bound of adversarial perturbations where the perturbations cause the model to misclassify but are not perceptible to human, the assumption that the size of the $\epsilon$ is small enough to only move the hard example but not large enough to move the easy example is the probable assumption ($\epsilon$ is not larger than the center of two examples). For the relationship between differences between $D_{std}$, $D_{adv}$, and $\epsilon$, because we already proved that the difference is monotonically decreasing for the input data, it leads to that the difference increases for $\epsilon$ in the same condition.

**Q**: The proposed algorithm DPLS is an incremental upgrade of label smoothing and is similar to self-adaptive training.I doubt the better performance of DPLS on A3 is a result of robust accuracy - clean accuracy trade-off. In addition, the improvement is marginal, the authors should run these experiments multiple time. \
**A**: As mentioned in Section 3.3, memorizing hard examples deteriorates robust accuracy but improves standard accuracy. Because our method regularizes the training of hard examples using smoothed labels, it leads to the regularization of the effect of hard examples that increased standard accuracy. Since we set the smoothing factor as 0.1, which is the minimum value for a 10-class dataset, the effect seems severe in this setting. The ablation study of the smoothing factor can be seen in Table 17, and it shows some trade-offs when the smoothing factor is low. However, the results demonstrate that when the smoothing factor is selected properly, our method improves robust accuracy without decreasing the standard performance. For the comparison to the KD+SWA model, we conducted it multiple times (additional three). Additionally, because our method is orthogonal to SWA [2], we trained the model with the method combining DPLS and SWA. From the below Table, although our method shows marginal improvement compared to KD+SWA [3], further improvement is observed when combined with SWA.

|                  PGD (+DPLS)                 |    85.95 $\pm$ 0.1922   |      57.8 $\pm$ 0.1850     |  53.61 $\pm$ 0.1113  |
|             PGD (+DPLS + SWA)            | 87.64 $\pm$ 0.18     | 59.94 $\pm$ 0.1769 |     55.31 $\pm$ 0.0472 |

content.title: Response to Reviewer HeMq (2/2)
content.comment:
Additionally, we connect the degradation of performance caused by hard examples to the memorization of data that function as label corrupted data, which is attributed to the significant increase in the difficulty of data in adversarial training. In this case, because the features of the data are not consistent with the one-hot label, we proposed to assign new labels directly using the difficulty score. None of the previous works addressed the deterioration of robust performance from this point of view. As a soft label method, DPLS is similar to existing methods. Previous methods calculate soft labels by using a temporal ensemble of the confidence of each example. However, our method is not limited to the temporal ensemble of confidence. For difficulty calculation, our method can use any loss which is an error measure of each example. DPLS is not simply a kind of soft label methodology, but a simple framework that can utilize difficulty for hard example mitigation, as can be seen in Table 5 in our paper. 

**Q**: The theory is not directly connected to robust overfitting. The theory only shows the difference of the gradient on a toy two-layer network. While the loss gradient norm is empirically connected to the hardness, it is not a rigorous theoretical result. \
**A**: Our theoretical analysis does not directly connect hard examples in adversarial training to robust overfitting. We demonstrated that memorizing hard examples is one of the main causes of deteriorating robust performance in adversarial training. Our theoretical analysis proves that the difficulty increases for hard examples are significant, resulting in data that function as labeled corrupted data. Because memorizing label corrupted data naturally deteriorates the performance, when the model starts to fit hard adversarial examples, the performance decreases as seen in Fig. 3b, representing overfitting. Although we conducted analysis on a simple model, we empirically proved our theoretical analysis for DNNs by measuring the approximate gradient norm of training examples in Section 3.2 (plotted in Fig. 4). We used the loss gradient norm as the hardness following [2], which we mentioned in our paper.

**Q**: The analyses in Section 3 use the EL2N score as the measurement of the difficulty. However, the experiments in Section 4 use 0-1 loss to measure the difficulty. It makes the two parts inconsistent. \
**A**: We employed 0-1 loss as the measure of difficulty in both Section 3 and Section 4, which we mentioned in our paper. We used the average loss of the model along the training trajectory, and because other losses such as EL2N are affected by training status (e.g. different average max confidence at epoch 1 and epoch 50), we selected 0-1 loss for the average difficulty of training trajectory.

[1] Chen Liu, Zhichao Huang, Mathieu Salzmann, Tong Zhang, and Sabine Süsstrunk. On the impact of hard adversarial instances on overfitting in adversarial training. arXiv preprint arXiv:2112.07324, 2021. \
[2] Mansheej Paul, Surya Ganguli, and Gintare Karolina Dziugaite. Deep learning on a data diet: Finding important examples early in training. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 34, 2021. \
[3] Lang Huang, Chao Zhang, and Hongyang Zhang. Self-adaptive training: beyond empirical risk minimization. Advances in neural information processing systems, 33:19365–19376, 2020. \
[4] Han Xu, Xiaorui Liu, Yaxin Li, Anil Jain, and Jiliang Tang. To be robust or to be fair: Towards fairness in adversarial training. In International Conference on Machine Learning, pp. 1149211501. PMLR, 2021.

Thank you for reviewing our manuscript and pointing out previous works which address the effect of hard examples in adversarial training. We would like to address your concerns and questions.

**Q**: The novelty of the paper is limited as the relationship between hard examples and robust overfitting has already been studied in [1]. While the paper cites this paper, its contribution is not fully recognized. And the main observations in the Section were provided in [1]. [1] already showed that overfitting the hard examples lead to robust overfitting. And that paper provides a more in-depth theoretical analysis of the phenomenon. \
**A**: The different point from [1] is that we focus on whether pruning certain examples can lead to improvement in test robustness. It is proven to be possible in standard training [2]. They demonstrated that pruning a small subset of examples with a high importance score shows higher performance than the model trained with a full dataset. In [1], they showed that hard examples lead to performance degradation, but they did not show that pruning hard examples from the training dataset improves or at least maintains robustness. For the method proposed in [1], because they do not provide the results for standard adversarial training (PGD), we compare the results of their methods (Reweight and Adaptive Target) with our methods. ([1]) denotes that the model is trained using the code and settings of [1]. It seems that Reweight is not applicable to the standard adversarial training and Adaptive Target shows the same performance as SAT [3] (because it is simply a linear combination of SAT and one-hot label).

content.title: Response to Reviewer mCYK
content.comment:
Thank you for reviewing our manuscript and indicating ambiguous parts in our theoretical analysis. We would like to address your concerns and questions.

**Q**: For the assumption 'the training loss of the classifier almost converges to the minimum', I guess it does not hold for adversarial training (e.g., on CIFAR-10/100). \
**A**: It does not hold when the model is trained with a high learning rate and not sufficiently trained. However, as plotted in Fig. 3c (CIFAR-10 adversarial training loss curve), after the learning rate decay epoch (epoch 100), the training loss significantly decreases and converges to approximately zero for all training example subsets including the hard example subset. Actually, "the training loss of the classifier almost converges to the minimum" is the assumption to guarantee that the gradient norm of easy examples is smaller than the gradient norm of hard examples in both standard and adversarial training. The assumption could be replaced with a relaxed condition for the above guarantee. Sorry for the confusion, we will correct the assumption with a more proper condition.

**Q**: For the assumption "we assume the norm of every input x is almost the same", it is far from reality. Alternatively, I think this work can consider a bound of ||x|| here; We normally use a final softmax layer in a DNN, I guess the theoretical result does not hold with a softmax layer; I guess the theoretical result does not hold for ReLU, by the way, what is the activation function in the experiment? \
**A**: The classification model in our theoretical analysis demonstrates that the increases in the difficulty of hard examples are more significant than those of easy examples. Because our model is defined as $f(x)=\sigma(w^Tx)$, $x$ corresponds to the penultimate layer output of the DNN. Here, softmax corresponds to the sigmoid function. For the question of ReLU, the models that are used in our experiment do not use ReLU activation function from the penultimate layer (WideResNet for CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN). For the assumption that the norm of every input x is almost the same, we measured the norm of the penultimate layer output of the training examples. We measured the norm using the models before the learning rate decay (epoch 99), right after the learning rate decay (epoch 101), and the final epoch (epoch 200) for 10k easy, 10k hard, and entire training examples. The below Table shows the norm of the penultimate layer outputs. As shown in the result of the Table, there are hardly differences between the norm of easy, hard, and entire examples in each model. Although easy and hard example subsets are class-imbalanced, they represent similar norms between subsets. The distributions of easy and hard example subset are plotted in Fig. 15.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work investigates the impact of hard examples on adversarial training of examples, in particular, how their removal changes the model's generalization performance. 
1. Hard examples are fit by a model via memorization.
2. This makes them much harder in adversarial training as opposed to standard training.
3. The increased difficulty of hard examples in an adversarial setting transforms hard examples into feature-corrupted data and decreases the performance
Based on these observations and conclusions, the authors propose "difficulty proportional label smoothing" (DPLS) to mitigate the negative impact of adversarial examples on the generalization performance of the model. The key contribution is that rather than only seeking extra data to improve adversarial training, the authors suggest that regularizing existing data can be 

Some interesting findings from this work:
1. Even changing labels of hard examples to random labels does not deteriorate the model's generalization.
2. A smoothing factor that is proportional to the difficulty of the example helps regularizing the training of each example.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Weaknesses
1. The abstract of this paper is extremely hard to parse. Relaxing the writing in the abstract, and other areas will do this work a world of good.
2. "In particular, a compelling finding among their observations motivates our study: memorizing hard-to-learn/irregular examples can deteriorate the generalization ability of DNNs." Past work has shown that memorization of hard examples can be essential for optimal generalization. Check out these papers: https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.05271 https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.03703. How do your findings compare to these?
3. In the section on Comparing the difficulty of hard examples: it seems that the difference in EL2N norm is not a good metric, rather the relative increase in EL2N norm should be plotted. Since the EL2N norms of clean examples are already lower it is natural to expect that the difference in the norm for adversarial examples of hard samples will increase by a larger proportion.
4. The term "memorization" is used very loosely. For example in Page 5 " These results suggest that the PGD model memorizes hard examples." There is no clear definition of memorization, and a result suggest that memorization is happening. This is very problematic in terms of both presentation style and understanding. I have a similar issue with throwing in such terms in intro/abstract.


## Strengths
1. The method can be added on to various adversarial training method and helps increase robust accuracy. This makes it complimentary to advances in adversarial training. (Table 6)
2. Exprimental study is comprehensive, across various adversarial perturbation region sizes, hard example identification method
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1. Can you use the term mislabeled data, rather than label corrupted data? at least when only briefly talking about it like in abstract and introduction.

2. Too much negative vspace has been used.

It is unclear to me if, in datasets with long tails of rare examples, their findings will hold or not. I have referred to relevant papers in my review above.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 68Wg
content.comment:
Thank you for reviewing our manuscript and indicating some ambiguous parts in our paper. We would like to address your concerns and questions.

**Q**: "In particular, a compelling finding among their observations motivates our study: memorizing hard-to-learn/irregular examples can deteriorate the generalization ability of DNNs." Past work has shown that memorization of hard examples can be essential for optimal generalization. Check out these papers: https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.05271 https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.03703. How do your findings compare to these? \
**A**: As mentioned in Section 3.3, memorization of certain examples that are the sole representative of a subpopulation can improve performance. Here, certain examples that are the sole representative can be hard examples, and training with the dataset which includes those examples increased the accuracy in standard training (plotted in Fig. 7). However, as explained in Section 3.2, hard examples function as label corrupted data (because of corrupted features). Although memorizing hard clean examples with correct labels can improve performance, memorizing hard adversarial examples with incorrect labels can deteriorate performance. Thus, “memorization of hard examples can be essential for optimal generalization” is consistent with our experimental results of standard accuracy but is inconsistent with those of robust accuracy. We found that the effects of memorization of hard examples are different between standard training and adversarial training, and our findings reveal that the effect of memorization of hard examples in adversarial training is negative.

**Q**: In the section on Comparing the difficulty of hard examples: it seems that the difference in EL2N norm is not a good metric, rather the relative increase in EL2N norm should be plotted. Since the EL2N norms of clean examples are already lower it is natural to expect that the difference in the norm for adversarial examples of hard samples will increase by a larger proportion. \
**A**: As indicated, the gradient norm of easy clean examples is already lower than that of hard clean examples because the difficulty of easy examples is naturally lower than that of hard examples. Here, we demonstrated that the increases in the difficulty when the training examples are transformed into adversarial examples are significant for hard examples. We used EL2N because it approximates the norm of the gradient of each example. The relative increases in EL2N norm of hard and easy examples are plotted in Fig. 4 (right column, comparison of $\epsilon=8$ hard difference and $\epsilon=8$ easy difference).

**Q**: The term "memorization" is used very loosely. For example, on Page 5, " These results suggest that the PGD model memorizes hard examples." There is no clear definition of memorization, and a result suggests that memorization is happening. This is very problematic in terms of both presentation style and understanding. I have a similar issue with throwing in such terms in the intro/abstract. \
**A**: For clarity on “memorization”, we measured the degree of memorization of training examples using the metric that is proposed in [1] in Section 3.2. We determined that the model memorizes training examples when the metric score represents high values. As shown in Fig. 6 (right), in adversarial training, because the score of hard examples converges to the maximum score (1.0), it suggests that the model fits hard examples only through memorization.

[1] Vitaly Feldman. Does learning require memorization? a short tale about a long tail. In Proceedings of the 52nd Annual ACM SIGACT Symposium on Theory of Computing, pp. 954–959, 2020.
